Even if he appointed him as an agent. The Shach inclines to accept Rashi's explanation that agency is effective. He understands this to mean that if the principal pays him and hires him for this agency, his status becomes that of a worker, whose hand is like the hand of his employer, and the Gemara states explicitly that he can acquire for the employer. In truth, Rashi's language, "since the creditor did not appoint him as an agent to acquire for him," sounds unlike the Shach, for Rashi should then have said, "since he did not hire him." Still, the Shach spoke correctly on this point. Rashi, who distinguishes between one whom he appointed as an agent and one whom he did not, derived this from the rule that a worker can acquire for his employer. Rashi understood that there is no relevant difference toward third parties between one who works for wages and one who acts gratuitously. What legal force is added by wages? He can say, "I regard myself as though I had already received my wages," and in any event the benefit of the principal's gratitude is itself worth a perutah. Rashi therefore held that the same rule applies to an agent. This also answers the question raised against Rashi: how could the Gemara challenge from the law of a worker if, according to Rashi, an agent can seize? According to what I have written, Rashi said this only after the Gemara answered, "a worker is different." From that answer Rashi learned that the same applies to an agent, since there is no substantive distinction between them. At the initial stage, however, even an agent would not have acquired. The Maharsha asks in Ketubot, in the chapter HaKotev, why Tosafot challenge Rashi from the incident of Yemar bar Chashu, who appointed an agent to seize and nevertheless was treated as one who seizes for a creditor where others are thereby harmed. Rashi may have said that agency helps only where the agent himself could acquire the property, as with a found object, whereas in the case of a debt, when the debtor owes nothing to the agent, Rashi never said this. The Maharsha writes that Tosafot did not accept such a distinction. It is true that Tosafot did not accept it, because Rashi's language, "the creditor did not appoint him as an agent," is stated without qualification and appears to include even an agent who has no personal claim against the debtor. Nevertheless, in my opinion this was unquestionably Rashi's intent. When we say that a worker's hand is like the employer's hand, that is in a found object, where the worker has a legal hand in the object himself. We can then say that his hand is treated as the employer's, so that his own acquisition becomes the employer's acquisition. But where the worker has no legal hand in the property at all, as with a debt that is not owed to him, how can we say that his hand is like the employer's when he has no hand in the property to begin with? This explains why Rashi wrote this only in Bava Metzia at the initial stage, when the discussion assumed that one who lifts a found object for another does not acquire it for the other. In such a setting Rashi writes that an agent is effective because he could acquire the object for himself. Once the Gemara concludes that with a found object the other person acquires in any event, Rashi nowhere distinguishes an agent in the law of creditors. How could this distinction be rejected entirely? The Mordechai in the first chapter of Chullin itself is uncertain whether a worker of the creditor may seize the creditor's debt. At first glance this is difficult, for the Gemara expressly says, "a worker is different, because his hand is like the hand of the employer." The Mordechai's doubt must therefore be precisely whether that rule applies only to a found object, in which the worker has an independent hand, or also to a creditor's property, in which he has none. The silence of the other authorities likewise indicates that an employee or hired worker of the creditor cannot seize the debtor's property merely because his hand is treated as the employer's. The Rif and the Rosh omit the Gemara's question and answer concerning a worker, apparently because they understood that this answer was not stated as practical law for a creditor's case. Accordingly, even a worker does not help with a debt, for the reason stated. To clarify further where Rashi's view tends, consider Rashi's explanation in Beitzah 39 concerning a public well. One drew water and gave it to another, and Rav Sheshet and Rav Nachman dispute whether the water follows the feet of the one who drew it or the one for whom it was drawn. The Gemara initially suggests that they disagree whether the well is ownerless or jointly owned. Rashi explains that if it is ownerless, we hold that one who lifts a found object for another does not acquire it for the other because he is seizing for one creditor to the detriment of others, while the one who lifts it acquires it himself. Rav Nachman, however, holds that the well is jointly owned by all Israel. When the other person told him to draw from his share and he went on his agency, the drawer became his agent, and this is not a case of lifting a found object for another. This seems to show that according to Rav Sheshet, who treats the well as ownerless, even though the drawer was acting as an agent, the intended recipient does not acquire. That would contradict what I have attributed to Rashi, namely that agency itself suffices. At first I considered answering by asking why Rashi had to say that the other person appointed him as an agent to draw at all. Perhaps he simply drew for his fellow without any appointment. Rashi may have been troubled that, even at the conclusion, the entire sugya would then be contrary to the halakhah. We rule that one who lifts a found object for another acquires it for the other. On Rashi's approach, everyone should therefore agree that the water follows the feet of the person for whom it was drawn, eliminating the dispute. It would also nearly produce a contradiction in practical rulings, since we rule like Rabbi Yochanan that one who lifts a found object for another acquires it for him, yet in matters of prohibition we rule like Rav Sheshet, who says that the water follows the feet of the drawer, implying that the recipient did not acquire it. Rashi therefore explains that the drawer was indeed made an agent, but the instruction was "draw for me," not "acquire for me." Even according to Rabbi Yochanan this is inferior, and the recipient does not acquire, as is clear from the Mishnah in Bava Metzia where one says, "give it to me," rather than "acquire it for me." In such a case his words make matters worse, and silence would have been better. The present sugya can therefore concern that same case. All agree that the recipient does not acquire, and the dispute is whether the drawer acquires it. This is how Rashi explains both the initial stage and the conclusion. There is therefore no difficulty, and Rashi can concede that an agent who was told merely "give it to me" does not acquire for the principal. This also helps explain Tosafot's question on Rashi in the passage beginning HaBa. According to Rashi, at the conclusion Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet agree that the person for whom the water was drawn does not acquire it, and they dispute only whether the drawer acquires it for himself. Tosafot object that it is unreasonable for the drawer to acquire for himself without intending to do so. Rabbenu Tam therefore explains that Rav Sheshet holds that the recipient acquires through the migo that the drawer could have acquired for himself. Consequently, the recipient cannot have a broader techum right in the water than the drawer himself could have had. Rav Nachman holds that the recipient does not acquire it and it remains ownerless. Tosafot also cite Rashbam's explanation that Rav Nachman holds that the recipient does acquire because, with water from a well, there is no detriment to others, so Rav Nachman does not contradict his own general rule. See there. Yet according to Rashbam, Tosafot's original objection would still remain under Rashi's conclusion. If the recipient does not acquire, why should the water follow the drawer because the drawer acquired it for himself when he never intended to do so? One could answer that Rashbam too accepts Rabbenu Tam's principle that where the recipient acquires only through the migo that the drawer could acquire for himself, the recipient cannot acquire rights broader than those of the drawer. Rashbam merely considered it strained to explain "like the feet of the person for whom it was drawn" on the ground that the water remained ownerless, because the language implies that the recipient acquired immediately upon the drawing, even if another person sought to acquire it before it reached him. Rashbam therefore explains that Rav Nachman holds that in water, where there is no detriment to others, one who lifts for another acquires for him directly, without the migo of his own ability to acquire. The water is accordingly immediately like the feet of the recipient. Rav Sheshet, however, agrees in practical law with Rabbi Yochanan only through the migo, and therefore the water remains like the feet of the drawer, as Rabbenu Tam explains. Tosafot in Bava Metzia bring these two explanations in Rabbenu Tam's name, which supports this reading. Nevertheless, whether according to Rashbam or Rabbenu Tam, a difficulty remains at the initial stage. There the Gemara says that Rav Nachman views the well as jointly owned and Rav Sheshet views it as ownerless, and for that reason Rav Sheshet says that the water follows the drawer. Tosafot's question returns: how does the drawer acquire it without intending to acquire? At the initial stage we cannot say that the recipient acquires only through the migo described above. According to Rabbenu Tam that explanation arises only at the conclusion. At the initial stage Rav Nachman holds that one who lifts a found object for another does not acquire for the other even where he has the migo. Rav Sheshet at that stage must therefore agree on that general rule, unless we make them disagree about two separate matters, both whether lifting a found object for another works and whether the well is jointly owned or ownerless, which is implausible. It would then follow that the drawer himself acquires, reviving Tosafot's objection. If there is a satisfactory answer at the initial stage, the same answer should seemingly remain available at the conclusion according to Rashi, for the Gemara never retracted that underlying reasoning. This requires study. According to what I have written, however, the matter is resolved. One must first understand the force of Tosafot's question, "how can he acquire for himself without intent?" It is reasonable that when a person takes ownerless property intending to acquire it for another, if the other cannot acquire through him, he should acquire it himself. Shitah Mekubetzet to Bava Metzia indeed cites this in the name of the Rosh. Tosafot's difficulty comes from the Mishnah: one saw a found object, lifted it, and said, "I acquired it," he acquires it. The implication is that he acquires only because he expressly says "I acquired it," but not automatically. According to the view that one who lifts a found object for another does not acquire for the other, and if the Mishnah is not limited to a case where he had earlier announced a contrary intent, why should the Mishnah require him to say "I acquired it"? It should simply say that the lifter acquires. The Mishnah thus implies that one who lifts it for another does not ordinarily acquire it for himself merely because the other failed to acquire. The distinction is that if he independently lifts ownerless property, we may presume that he lifted it in order that someone acquire it. His immediate intention was to benefit his fellow, but if the fellow cannot acquire, he acquires it himself. By contrast, if he lifted it because his fellow commanded him and appointed him as an agent, he never lifted it for his own purposes at all. He lifted it solely for the fellow and pursuant to the fellow's instruction. Even if the principal fails to acquire, the agent has nevertheless performed the agency he accepted. Why should the agent now acquire for himself when that was not the purpose for which he lifted it? This fits well. According to Rabbenu Tam and Rashbam, the case of drawing water for another is not one where the recipient instructed the drawer and appointed him as agent. Their conclusion can therefore remain consistent with halakhah, because the recipient does acquire. At the initial stage, if the recipient does not acquire, we may still say that the drawer acquires for himself because he did not draw in vain. The Mishnah concerning a found object does not contradict this, because there the person lifted it pursuant to his fellow's instruction, as it says, "he said to him, give it to me." In such a case the lifter does not automatically acquire it for himself until he says, "I acquired it." But according to Rashi, who must understand the water case as one of agency in order to keep the sugya consistent with practical halakhah, Tosafot properly object that the drawer cannot acquire for himself without intent because he acted pursuant to the principal's instruction. This also explains the Mishnah. However, all this remains strained within Rashi. If so, at the conclusion Rashi should have expressly explained that the case involved agency and clarified carefully that the principal said only "draw for me" and not "acquire for me." This distinction could also answer Tosafot's challenge to Rashi from the incident of Yemar bar Chashu regarding the ketubah, because there the creditor told the agent to go seize and effectively said "bring it to me," not "acquire it for me." All of Tosafot's objections would then be resolved. Therefore the true explanation appears different. Rashi was compelled to explain at the initial stage that the person appointed the drawer as an agent because he was troubled by the question raised by the authorities: if one lifts a found object for another and the other does not acquire, while the lifter himself does acquire, how can the Mishnah concerning one who gathers peah for a poor person say that he must give it to the first poor person he encounters? The gatherer himself should acquire the peah. If so, he should be obligated to give it specifically to the poor person whom he originally named, because his verbal commitment is charity and is binding upon him like a vow. Or Zarua answers that the gatherer was wealthy. See there. Accordingly, Rav Nachman, who says that the dispute in the peah Mishnah applies even from one poor person on behalf of another and who holds that one who lifts a found object for another does not acquire for him, must also hold that the lifter himself does not acquire automatically. This produces a difficulty at the conclusion. Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet truly disagree, and Rav Sheshet too understands the peah Mishnah as applying from one poor person for another. Yet according to Rashi both agree that the intended recipient does not acquire. How then can Rav Sheshet say that the lifter does acquire? The problem is even stronger at the initial stage, where they are said to disagree whether the well is jointly owned or ownerless. We cannot reasonably say that they also disagree about a second issue concerning whether the lifter himself acquires. If they agree with Rav Nachman that he does not, then even if the well is ownerless, how can the drawer acquire the water? Rashi therefore understood that Rabbenu Tam's underlying principle is certainly correct: when one who lifts a found object for another acquires for the other only through the migo that he could acquire it for himself, the recipient cannot receive broader techum rights than the lifter. Rashi further understood that Rav Sheshet's statement here, that the recipient does not acquire and the water follows the drawer, does not mean that Rav Sheshet rejects Rabbi Yochanan's rule that one who lifts a found object for another acquires for him. If that were so, practical rulings would contradict one another. Rather, the ordinary rule is based on the principle that one may acquire for a person in his absence. That principle works where the acquisition benefits the recipient. Here, however, if the drawer did not acquire the water for him until it reached his possession, the water would follow the recipient's feet. By acquiring it for him earlier, the drawer causes him a disadvantage because it follows the drawer's feet as a stringency, while certainly also being restricted by the recipient's own feet as a stringency. Thus the earlier acquisition is a detriment to him, and the principle that one may acquire for another in his absence does not apply. Rashi therefore holds that the drawer himself acquires the water. The peah Mishnah is no difficulty, because it can concern a wealthy gatherer, while in ordinary cases Rav Sheshet holds like Rabbi Yochanan that one who lifts a found object for another acquires for him. We cannot say that the water case involved an appointed agent, because then the rule against causing detriment to another would not apply, since the acquisition was made with the recipient's consent. Moreover, Rav Nachman's reason that the water follows the recipient would become impossible. Rashi holds that an appointed agent acquires for the principal where the agent himself has a legal hand with which to acquire, as the Maharsha understood Rashi. Rabbenu Tam's principle would then return: the principal cannot receive more extensive rights than the agent could acquire for himself. How could the water have a broader techum than the agent's own techum? The case therefore cannot be one of agency at the conclusion. The drawer acted on his own, and for this reason Rashi does not read the sugya as saying that the recipient acquired directly. The dispute is then coherent. At the initial stage, however, there remains a difficulty. If the well is ownerless, Rav Nachman would agree with Rav Sheshet, yet Rav Nachman holds that the peah dispute applies even between poor people, which indicates that the lifter himself does not acquire when the intended recipient fails to acquire. Rav Sheshet must then likewise hold that absent acquisition by the recipient, the drawer would not acquire. For this reason, at the initial stage Rashi had to explain the case as one in which the recipient told him to draw. In that circumstance everyone agrees that the recipient acquires. Rav Sheshet nevertheless says that the water follows the drawer, based on Rabbenu Tam's principle that the recipient cannot have greater rights than the agent through whom he acquires. Rav Nachman would agree to this rule in a genuine agency case, but at the initial stage he holds that the well is jointly owned and therefore reaches a different result. Rashi's words are thus precise and thoroughly coherent. There are not two independent disputes either at the initial stage or at the conclusion. This also explains why Tosafot did not challenge Rashi at the initial stage on the ground that the drawer could not acquire without intent. At that stage, Rashi understood the case as one of actual agency, and on this point his approach is the same as Rabbenu Tam's. It therefore appears that there is substantial basis for the explanation of Rashi given above, namely that Rashi did not state the agency rule as the final law concerning a creditor. I can add another support. Rashi's view that an agent can certainly acquire at the initial stage follows from the rule of a protected courtyard where the owner is not standing beside it. Such a courtyard acquires through the law of agency. If an agent could not acquire a found object for the principal, how could a courtyard acquire a found object for its owner through agency? Rashi therefore held that a true agent can acquire, at least at that stage of the sugya. Once we rule, however, that with a found object the recipient acquires through the migo that the lifter could acquire for himself, the courtyard acquires independently in any event. Although a courtyard cannot literally have a migo of acquiring for itself, the Torah equated it to an agent. At the initial stage, by contrast, if an actual agent could never acquire a found object for the principal, it would be impossible for a courtyard to acquire a found object by virtue of agency when the very agent to whom it is compared could not do so. See Shitah Mekubetzet in the sugya discussing whether courtyard is derived from the law of one's hand and is no worse than agency. It cites authorities who reason that one cannot invoke agency for a found object because even a full agent cannot acquire such an object. Ritva, however, concludes in accordance with Rashi that a protected courtyard functions like an agent and does acquire a found object. This supports Rashi's approach. See also below, siman 248, seif 3 and Sema seif katan 6, that a courtyard acquires a found object through agency. I found a further explicit indication in Bava Kamma 70, in the dispute concerning a power of attorney and whether the representative is treated as an agent. Rashi writes according to the version that if the representative seized property of the defendant, it is removed from him because he is one who seizes for a creditor in a manner that harms others. Rashi thus states clearly that even an agent cannot seize for a creditor. It is therefore certain that Rashi did not state his Bava Metzia explanation as the final law for creditors. Mahara Sasson writes that Ritva in Gittin accepted Rashi's explanation, but that text is not before us. Ritva to Bava Metzia expressly rules unlike that broad reading of Rashi and holds that even an agent cannot seize. Who knows which formulation represents his later view? In any event, we should not depart from Tosafot, the other authorities, and the ruling of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch. As for the Mordechai's uncertainty regarding a worker in a creditor's case, this too requires study, as stated. The other decisors omit it, for the reason I explained: the rule applies specifically where the worker himself has a legal hand in the property. It is strained to say that now that we rule that one who lifts a found object for another acquires for him, we no longer need Rav Nachman's answer that "a worker is different." Why invent a new dispute against an explicit statement of Rav Nachman when no contrary opinion is found? At first glance one might instead argue that a worker hired specifically to collect found objects cannot acquire them for himself at all and has no independent hand of acquisition, because his hand is entirely directed toward his employer. If he truly had the power to acquire each found object for himself, and merely had a contractual duty to hand it over to the employer because that was the purpose of his employment, what was the Gemara's question from the teaching that a worker's found object belongs to his employer? One could say that the worker first acquired it personally and the teaching merely tells us that he must afterward transfer it to the employer pursuant to their agreement. The Gemara's question therefore implies that one hired to gather found objects has no independent hand to acquire them for himself at all, only for the employer. If so, he has no migo of personal acquisition. This also explains another point. Rav Nachman and Rav Chisda both say that one who lifts a found object for another does not acquire it for the other, yet Rabbah challenges Rav Nachman specifically from the baraita concerning a worker's found objects. Why does he not challenge Rav Chisda as well, since both stated the same rule? According to the foregoing, Rav Chisda can answer that the baraita follows Rabbi Eliezer, who holds in the peah case that the gatherer acquires for the poor person. One might object that there the gatherer has a migo because he could acquire for himself, whereas a worker lacks any such migo. But Rav Chisda himself holds in the first chapter of Gittin that according to Rabbi Eliezer one may acquire for a poor person even without any migo. Rav Nachman, however, says, "let the master say that the dispute is from one poor person for another," rather than saying "even from one poor person for another." Since Rabbi Eliezer clearly permits even a wealthy person to gather for a poor person, this wording suggests that Rav Nachman understands Rabbi Eliezer as requiring a migo. Rabbah can therefore challenge Rav Nachman from the worker baraita, and the Gemara answers that a worker is different. Tosafot, however, in the passage beginning VeLeima, conclude that according to Rabbi Eliezer even Rav Nachman does not require a migo, because Rav Chisda, who agrees with Rav Nachman's general rule, says in the first chapter of Gittin that Rabbi Eliezer does not require one. Their intent is not merely that two amoraim who agree on one point must agree on every detail. Rather, Tosafot regard it as an unnecessary dispute to make Rav Nachman and Rav Chisda disagree about Rabbi Eliezer when no evidence requires such a disagreement. Since Rav Chisda says that Rabbi Eliezer does not require a migo, the same should be presumed for Rav Nachman unless compelled otherwise. One should not say that Rabbi Eliezer's position would then become too extreme, since the Sages deny acquisition even from one poor person for another where a migo exists, whereas Rabbi Eliezer would allow a wealthy person with no migo to acquire for a poor person. Rav Chisda himself accepts precisely that broad dispute, so there is no reason Rav Nachman could not as well. But why did Tosafot need to establish whether, according to Rav Nachman, Rabbi Eliezer requires a migo? We do not rule like Rav Nachman on the general issue, nor do we rule like Rabbi Eliezer. The point must be to exclude the proposed answer that the worker baraita follows Rabbi Eliezer. Had that answer been available, the fact that the Gemara did not use it would prove that a worker lacks any migo, and then one could argue that his hand is nevertheless like his employer's even in a creditor's case. Tosafot show, however, that Rabbi Eliezer does not require a migo even according to Rav Nachman. The question would therefore remain: why not establish the baraita like Rabbi Eliezer? We must say that the Gemara knew the baraita was stated in accordance with the practical halakhah. It is then still possible that a worker does have a hand with which to acquire a found object, and therefore has a migo; it is only in that setting that we say his hand is like the employer's. In a creditor's case, where the worker has no personal right at all because the debtor owes him nothing, the rule does not apply. Tosafot thereby teach us a substantial point. This also appears to exclude the broad reading of Rashi. Once Tosafot establish that the baraita cannot simply be assigned to Rabbi Eliezer, the original question remains: why was Rav Nachman challenged and not Rav Chisda? According to Rav Chisda one can invoke Rashi's distinction that an agent is different, and a worker is certainly no worse than an agent. The Mishnah that says "I acquired it" can be understood as meaning that he said, "I had acquired it for myself from the outset." Rav Nachman, however, says that the peah dispute extends from one poor person for another and brings proof from the Mishnah. He therefore cannot interpret "I acquired it" as meaning "I acquired it from the outset," and it follows that even an agent does not acquire automatically. He can thus be challenged from the worker baraita, and the Gemara answers that a worker is different and has a stronger status than an ordinary agent. This is unlike the Shach, who equates the two. Tosafot therefore also undermine the claim that Rashi equates an agent with a worker as final law. I have expanded somewhat in order to clarify the sugya. For practical halakhah, since the decisors omit any special power of a worker in the creditor context, the implication is as I have written: only with a found object, where the worker himself has a legal hand, can his hand be treated as the employer's. With a creditor, however, even a worker may not seize to the detriment of other creditors.
And he gave him a power of attorney. The Bach writes that an authorized representative may seize property, and the Shach disagrees. The matter does require study, because I found in Shitah Mekubetzet to Bava Metzia, quoting the Tosafot HaChitzonim, precisely the Bach's view that one who holds a formal power of attorney may seize. The incident of Yemar bar Chashu involving a ketubah concerned a person who had no such authorization. Likewise, in Bava Kamma 70 the Gemara discusses a representative who seized property. Rashi explains one version that if he seized property belonging to the defendant, even though the authorization did not contain the words "go litigate and recover for yourself," the property is not removed from him. Rav Ashi disagrees and says that the principal merely appointed him as an agent. Rashi explains on that version that if he seized property belonging to the defendant it is removed from him because he is one who seizes for a creditor where that seizure harms others. This indicates that had the authorization expressly said "go litigate and recover for yourself," he would indeed have been able to seize, and would not be considered merely one seizing for another creditor. Nimukei Yosef also records this version, so the point is explicit that a fully authorized representative can seize. It therefore appears necessary to distinguish between a debt that, under the law of the Gemara, is itself transferable through a power of attorney, as explained below in siman 122, and a claim for which authorization works only by later enactment. In the first case the representative acquires a direct litigating right and is effectively a party himself, so the rule against seizing for a creditor where others are harmed does not apply. In the second case the legal ownership does not truly pass to him, and the authorization works only because he is treated as the principal's agent, as Tosafot, the Rosh, and many other authorities explain. He then has no greater power than any other agent and may not seize to the detriment of other creditors. This distinction is clear and correct for halakhah.

urim_vetumim_urim.he:
לא זכה והרי הוא כאלו עדיין ביד הלוה ויש לכל המלוים זכיה בו מבלי הבדל ואע"ג דקי"ל זכין לאדם שלא בפניו ה"מ כשאמר לו הלוה זכי לו או שאין חב לאחרים אבל בלא"ה לא דאין לו יד לזכות לזה ולחוב לזה סמ"ע:
שכל התופס וכו' ואפילו הוא אצלו בפקדון א"י ג"כ לתפוס בשביל אחד במקום שחב לאחרים דהרי הוא כמונח ברשות הלוה עיין כה"ג:
ואפילו עשהו שליח דעת מהר"א ששון בתשובה דיוכל המוחזק לומר קים לי כרש"י דבעשהו שליח מהני והש"ך מחלק בין שכרו ללא שכרו ואני העליתי בתומים דאין חילוק ולעולם לא זכה ואף רש"י לא אמרו אלא בס"ד לא למסקנא גם העליתי דנראה מסתימת הפוסקים דאפילו היה אצל בעל הבית פועל ותפס משל לוה לא מהני לגבי חוב הואיל ולית ליה לפועל אצל הלוה כלום עיין שם:
הרשאה ודעת הב"ח דבהרשאה יכול לתפוס והש"ך חולק ואני בתומים כתבתי דנראין דברי הב"ח בהרשאה דמהני מדינא כדלקמן סי' קכ"ב אבל במה דלא מהני מדינא רק מכח תקנה ושליח שוי' חד דינא אית ליה כמו שליח.
urim_vetumim_urim.en:
He did not win, and he was still in the hands of the Levites, and all the words of the Levites in him have no difference, and he has no hand for the man who did not have the “meet” when he told him that he had no desire for others, but that he did not give him a hand to receive it and owe it to it a “signment”:
All the groves and so on, and even if he is in possession of the High Court to seize for one place where he is drawn to others, he is as a guide to the Leviathan Authority:
Even if he appointed him as agent. Rabbi Aharon Sasson holds in responsum that the possessor can say he is certain like Rashi that appointment as agent makes the seizure effective. The Shach distinguishes whether the agent was paid. In Tumim I concluded that there is no such distinction. The seizure never transfers title, and even Rashi's suggestion appears only in the preliminary discussion, not in the final conclusion. I further concluded from the unqualified language of the authorities that even if the agent is already employed by the creditor and seizes property from the debtor, the seizure does not help for the creditor's debt, because the agent himself has no claim against the debtor. See there.
Authorization. Bach holds that seizure under a formal authorization is effective. The Shach disagrees. In Tumim I wrote that Bach's view appears correct where the authorization is legally effective by strict law, as explained below in siman 122. But where the authorization itself has no strict legal force and is recognized only because of a rabbinic enactment, it has the same law as ordinary agency and does not improve the seizure.

mechaber.he: אם הלוה חייב גם לתופס זכה בתפיסתו מגו דאי בעי זכי לנפשיה זכי לחבריה:
mechaber.en: If the bride also owes him a glimpse of his body from his hands in the face of his soul, he will be blessed to her friends:

baer_hetev.he: לתופס. כת' הסמ"ע דהיינו דוקא שתפס בכדי חובו כגון שמגיע לכל אחד ק' זהובים ותפס שוה ק' זהו' בזה אמרינן ל"מ אם תפס בשבילו ובשביל חבירו לכל אחד נ' זהובים דאמרי' מגו כו' אלא אפי' תפס כל הסך לחבירו לחוד אמרי' נמי מגו דאי בעי הי' תופס לנפשו שהרי מגיע לו גם כן סך זה אבל אם תפס שוה ק"נ זהובים ורוצה לזכות בהמותר לחבירו לא מהני כיון דלא מצי הוא לזכות בכל הסך וראי' שהרי דין זה נלמד מהמגביה מציא' לחבירו דקנה חבירו משום דאי בעי זכי לנפשיה כו' ובעינן דומיא דהתם דאי בעי הי' זוכה בכולו וזהו דלא כמ"ש בב"י כיון דאית ביה צד זכייה לנפשיה מהני וגם בע"ש פסק כן ודבריהם דחויין הן בעיני עכ"ל וכת' הש"ך דגם בתשובת מ"ב האריך להשיג על הב"י והע"ש בזה אבל הוא דחה דבריהם והסכים עם הב"י והע"ש ע"ש ובתשובת מהרשד"ם סימן שפ"א:
baer_hetev.en: For the one who seizes. The Sema writes that this applies only where he seized an amount equal to his own debt. For example, if each creditor is owed one hundred gold coins and he seized property worth one hundred, then not only where he seized fifty for himself and fifty for his fellow do we apply the migo that he could have seized for himself, but even if he seized the entire one hundred solely for his fellow, the migo applies because he himself was entitled to seize that entire amount. If, however, he seized one hundred fifty and seeks to acquire the excess for his fellow, it is ineffective, since he could not have acquired the entire amount for himself. The Sema proves this from the law of one who lifts a found object for another, whose acquisition is effective because he could have acquired the entire object for himself. This is unlike the Beit Yosef and Levush, who hold that any possibility of acquisition for oneself is enough. The Shach notes that Responsa Masat Binyamin also challenges the Beit Yosef and Levush, but the Shach rejects those objections and agrees with the Beit Yosef and Levush. See also Responsa Maharashdam, siman 381.

beer_hagolah.he: ב"מ דף ט' ע"ב משמע דלכ"ע אמרינן הכי
beer_hagolah.en: Bava Metzia 9b implies that everyone agrees to this rule.

beur_hagra.he: אם הלוה חייב. ב"מ שם אר"י המגביה כו' וע"ש בתוס' ד"ה אר"י ובגטין שם בתוס' וכן בכתובות בתוס' שם:
beur_hagra.en: If the borrower owes. This follows Bava Metzia, where Rabbi Yochanan states the law of one who takes possession for a creditor. See Tosafot there, in Gittin, and in Ketubot.

chelkat_mechokek.he: ואם מכרה לבעל'. ה"ה נתנה או מחלה לבעל' כמ"ש בסמוך סעיף ד':
chelkat_mechokek.en: And if she sold her husband. The “gives or illness to the husband” as a “subjecture” near section 4:

ketzot_hachoshen.he: מיגו דזכי לנפשיה ע' ב"י וסמ"ע וש"ך היכ' שתופס יותר מכדי חובו ולענ"ד נרא' כדברי הב"י דאפי' בתופס יותר מכדי חובו אמרי' מיגו דזכי לנפשי' דהא בשליח לדבר עביר' דודאי לא הוי שליח ואפ"ה בשותפין שגנבו היכ' דגנב אדעתיה דידי' ואדעתי' דחברי' מהני משום מגו דזכה לנפשי' בחציו זכה נמי לחברי' אפי' במקום דליכ' שליחות כגון בגניב' דהוי דבר עביר' וכמבואר להדיא בפ"ק דמציע' דף ד' וע"ש ברש"י וא"כ כיון דאי הוי תפיס אדעתי' דידיה ואדעתי' דחברי' הוי מועיל אפי' ביתר מכדי חובו משום מגו דזכי לנפשי' זכה נמי לחברי' דמהני אפי' בדבר עביר' וכ"ש בזה א"כ אפי' תופס כולו אדעתי' דחברי' אמרינן תרי מגו ודו"ק ועמ"ש בסי' שמ"ח סעיף ח' מיהו היכא דתופס כולו אדעתי' דחברי' אפשר דלא אמרינן תרי מגו דהא קי"ל כרבנן גבי מי שליקט את הפיאה ואמר הרי זו לפ' עני דסברי רבנן דיתננה לעני הנמצא ראשון וא"כ מעשר לעני הוא דהא מעני לעני אמרי' מגו דזכי לנפשי' ואם כן ע"כ תרי מגו לא אמרי' מיהו הב"י מיירי דזוכ' אדעתי' ואדעתי' דחברי' וצ"ע:
ketzot_hachoshen.en:
Since he could acquire for himself. Beit Yosef, Sema, and Shach discuss whether one who has his own claim may seize more than the amount owed to him and thereby benefit another creditor. In my view Beit Yosef is correct that the principle "since he can acquire for himself, he can acquire for another" can extend even beyond the amount of his personal claim.

We see this with partners who commit theft. Ordinarily there is no agency for a transgression, yet where one thief takes for himself and his fellow, his acquisition can work for both through the principle that because he acquires his own share he can acquire the other's share. The mechanism therefore has force even where ordinary agency is unavailable.

Accordingly, if a creditor could have seized a portion for himself and simultaneously intended to seize the rest for another creditor, the same principle can support the entire act even though his own claim is smaller.

The remaining question is where he seized the entire asset only for the other creditor and not at all for himself. One might try to use two successive extensions: since he could have acquired part for himself, he could have acquired part for the other, and because he could thereby have acquired for the other, perhaps the whole follows. That is doubtful. The law of peah suggests we do not stack the principle twice. The Sages say that one who gathers peah for a particular poor person may have to give it to the first poor person encountered, even though a poor person can sometimes acquire for another poor person through the fact that he could acquire for himself. This indicates that two levels of "since he could acquire" are not automatically combined. Beit Yosef's rule is strongest where the seizer actually intends some acquisition for himself together with the acquisition for the other creditor.

meirat_einayim.he: מגו דאי בעי זכי לנפשיה עפ"ר שם כתבתי והוכחתי דהיינו דוקא דתפס בכדי חובו של עצמו כגון ראובן שחייב לשמעון ולוי ויהודה לכל אחד מאה זהובים ותפס שמעון מראובן שוה מאה זהובים דבזה אמרי' ל"מ אם תפסו בשבילו ובשביל לוי שכל א' יקח מהתפיסה חמשים זהובים דאמרי' מגו דמהני תפיס' לנפשיה מהני נמי גבי לוי אלא אפי' תפס כל המאה בשביל לוי לחוד אמרי' מגו דאי בעי היה תופס כל המאה לנפשו שהרי חייב לו ג"כ מאה מהני נמי גבי לוי אבל אם תפס משל ראובן שוה ק"ן זהובים ורוצה לזכות בהמותר מהחובו ללוי לא מהני כיון דלנפשיה לא מצי לזכות בכולו שהרי חובו אינו אלא מאה. וא' מהראיות הוא שהרי דין זה נלמד מהא דאמרי' המגביה מציאה לחבירו קנה חבירו משום דאי בעי זכי לנפשיה כו' ובעינן דומיא דהתם דאי בעי היה זוכה כולו לנפשיה ע"ש ודו"ק וזהו דלא כמ"ש הב"י דגם בזה אמרי' דמהניא התפיסה לחבירו כיון דאית ביה צד זכייה לנפשיה וגם בע"ש פסק כן ודברים דחויין הן בעיני:
meirat_einayim.en: By virtue of a migo that, had he wished, he could have acquired it for himself. In the Perishah I proved that this applies specifically where the amount seized does not exceed the seizer's own debt. For example, Reuven owes Shimon, Levi, and Yehudah one hundred gold coins each, and Shimon seizes property from Reuven worth one hundred. If Shimon seized it for himself and Levi, each may take fifty, because since the seizure would be effective for Shimon himself it is also effective for Levi. Even if Shimon seized the entire hundred solely for Levi, it is effective, because he could have seized the entire hundred for himself. But if Shimon seizes property worth one hundred fifty and seeks to acquire for Levi the fifty beyond his own debt, it is ineffective as to the surplus, because he himself could not have acquired the entire amount, his own debt being only one hundred. One proof is that this rule is derived from the law that one who lifts a lost object for another acquires it for the other because, had he wished, he could have acquired it for himself. The cases must be comparable, meaning he could have acquired the entire object for himself. This is unlike the Beit Yosef, who writes that the seizure for another is effective even beyond the seizer's own debt because there exists at least some possibility of acquisition for himself. The Ir Shushan follows that view. In my opinion, those words are rejected.

netivot_hamishpat_beurim.he: ואפי' עשאו שליח. עש"ך ס"ק א' שהאריך ליישב דברי רש"י שכתב דבעשאו שליח מהני אפי' במקום שחב לאחריני דכוונת רש"י הוא בשכרו להיות שליח ומש"ה מהני אפי' במקום דחב לאחריני משום דהוי כפועל דיד פועל כיד בעה"ב ע"ש ואישתמיטתי' דברי המרדכי פ"ק דחולין שנסתפק אי פועל יכול לתפוס חוב של בעה"ב והביאו התומים. ולפענד"נ דאין הפועל יכול לתפוס במקום דחב לאחריני הנה לכאור' קשה כיון דהא דפועל יכול לתפוס לאו מטעם שליחות הוא דהא שליחות לא מהני במקום דחב לאחריני ופועל מהני מטעם דידו כיד בעה"ב א"כ אפי' באותן דלאו בני שליחות נינהו כגון חש"ו שהן פועלים ג"כ מקנה מציאה לבעה"ב ולא אישתמיט שום פוסק לכתוב כן. לכן נראה דהעיקר כהתומים דלא אמרו יד הפועל כיד בעה"ב אלא במקום דיכול לזכות לנפשיה וכמ"ש המהרש"א בכתובות פ' הכותב והטעם נראה כיון דהפועל יכול לזכות לנפשיה א"כ הבעה"ב מידו דפועל קא זכי מש"ה בחש"ו שאינם זוכים לנפשם גם בעה"ב לא קנה מידם. ולפ"ז' בעכו"ם פועל אפשר דמהני (אמנם לפמ"ש במקום אחר דיאוש קנה גבי מציאה דנלמד מקרא דעל שה ועל שלמה כמ"ש התוס' בב"ק ס"ו דבעינ' אתי ליד זוכה דבקרא כתיב ומצאת' דאתי לידיה משמע נרא' כיון דבקרא כתיב לכל אבידת אחיך אין העכו"ם קונה אבידה ביאוש. ולפ"ז אף כשהוא פועל לא קנה) ולפי סברא זו לענין תופס לבע"ה דאין להפועל יד לזכות בו לא שייך לומר ידו כיד בעה"ב וכן הסכים התומים ובעיקר יישוב דברי רש"י נראה דהנה הנ"י בב"מ במשנ' דראה אותן רצין כתב וז"ל וחצר המשתמרת דלא בעינן שיהא עומד בצד שדהו צריכ' טעמא דהא לאו משום יד הוא דמהני כמו בגט דחתם בעי מצד חציר' כדלקמן וגם לא מטעם שליחות מטעם הרנב"ר ז"ל שא"א לזכות לחבירו מתורת שליחות אלא א"כ נעשה שלוחו של בעל הממון ובמציאה ליכא בעל הממון שיהיה זה שלוחו ולא שייך למימר בחצר כדאמרי' גבי מגבי' מציאה לחבירו דמגו דזכי לנפשיה זכי נמי לחבירו עכ"ל. והנה לכאורה קשה על הנ"י דאמאי לא קאמר כלישנ' דהש"ס דהוי תופס לבע"ח במקום שחב לאחריני דהא הר"ן ס"ל דבמקום שחב לאחריני אפי' עשאו שליח לא מהני. ונרא' דהוכרח לכך דהא הפ"י כתב הטעם דלא מהני שליחות במקום דחב לאחריני משום דהוי כשליח לדבר עבירה ובב"מ דף י"א מסיק הש"ס דבחצר מהני מטעם שליחות אף לדבר עביר' ממש כמו בגניבה דהוי דבר עבירה וחב לאחריני מש"ה הוכרח הר"ן לומר טעם אחר דהיינו דלא מהני בממון רק שליחות של בעל הממון והא דלא קאמר בש"ס טעם הר"ן גבי מגבי' מציאה לחבירו אי משום דר"ן ס"ל דזכי' לאו מטעם שליחות הוא ומהני אפי' במקום דלא מהני שליחות והיה לו להיות מועיל אפי' במקום דליכא שליחות של בעל הממון מטעם זכיה לכך הוצרך בש"ס לומר דזכי' לא מהני במקום דחב לאחריני אך לכאור' הר"ן פליג על דברי התו' בב"מ דף ע"ב שכתבו וז"ל וי"ל דאפי' יוכל לזכות לחבירו במציאה הכא אין קבלתו מן הנכרי זוכה לישראל חבירו דנהי אם היה הנכרי מפקיד מעותיו היה יכול לזכות לחבירו השתא מיהא שהנכרי אינו מפקירן אלא בא לזכות במעותיו למלו' ע"י זה הלוה אין לו כח לזכות שא"כ היה הישראל מקבל שליחות של נכרי לזכות במעותיו של ישראל ואין שליחות לנכרי וה"ל להיות מותר אפילו העמידו אצל נכרי אי לאו דלחומר' אמרינן דיש שליחות לנכרי עכ"ל משמע לכאור' מדברי התו' דאפי' מטעם שליחות מהני בהפקר ומציאה אפי' למאן דלא ס"ל מגו דזכי הרי מבואר דהתו' לא ס"ל כהר"ן שכ' דלא מהני שליחות לקבל הממון לענין שיהי' השליח כיד המלוה כשמקבל הממון וכמו בגיטין וקדושין דאין הממון יוצא מרשות בעל הממון אם לא בשליחות בעל הממון וכ"ז שהבעל הממון לא עשאו שליח לזכות בו לאחר אף שנתנו ליד שליח קבלה של המלו' לא יצא מרשות הלוה ויכול הלוה ליקח אותו מיד השליח ומש"ה מותר שם גבי ריבית בב"מ משום דהוי מעותיו של עכו"ם עדיין אף שנתנו לשליח קבלה של הישראל ומ"מ כתבו התו' שם דבהפקר מהני שליחות כיון דליכא בעל הממון ולכאורה חולק על הר"ן. אך אחר העיון נרא' דלא פליגי כלל דכבר הארכתי במקום אחר לחלק בין הפקר ליאוש דהפקר יצא מרשות בעלים אף שלא אתי ליד זוכה והוא בעצמו צריך לחזור ולזכות בו משא"כ באבידה אחר ייאוש לא יצא מרשות בעלים קודם שבא ליד זוכ' מש"ה גבי הפקר כתבו התו' שפיר דמהני שליחות כיון דליכא בעל הממון כלל אבל גבי מציאה דקודם שבא ליד זוכה הוי של בעל (הממון) לא מהני בלא בעל הממון. ולפ"ז א"ש דברי רש"י דהנ' לכאורה קשה על הר"ן שכ' דבממון לא מהני שליחות בלא בעל הממון למאן דס"ל דזכי' מטעם שליחות א"כ בתופס לבע"ח במקום שאינו חב לאחרים אמאי קנה הא לא מהני שליחות בממון בלא בעל הממון ועכצ"ל כיון דהלוה לא מיקרי בעל הממון כלל כיון שהוא משועבד למלו' ולית ליה לאשתלומי ממקום אחר וגם בתפיס' של התופס לא יצא מרשות הלוה לגמרי דהא הרשות ביד הלוה עדיין לסלק בזוזי אחר רק שתופס לאלם השיעבוד ולא בעינן כלל בעל הממון רק במקום שמוציא מרשות בעל הממון, ולפ"ז שפיר כ' רש"י דעשאו שליח מהני דרש"י ס"ל דשליחות מהני אפי' במקום דחב לאחריני וטעם הר"ן דלא מהני שליחות בלא בעל הממון לא שייך גבי תופס לבע"ח כיון דהלוה לא מיקרי בעל הממון לענין שלא יועיל עד שיעשה הלוה שליח מטעם שכתבתי בתופס במקום שאינו חב לאחרים והמלו' האחר ודאי דלא נקרא בעל הממון מש"ח מהני שליחות משא"כ גבי מציא' שמורה רש"י דלא מהני שליחות דבמציא' איכא בעל הממון ולא מהני בלא בעל הממון כמש"ל. ולפ"ז לא קשה קושית הרא"ש שהקש' ממתני' דהי' רוכב דמיירי בעשאו שליח וכן קושית המפורשים מהא דמקש' הש"ס מברייתא דמציאת פועל דהוי ע"י שליחות דבמציא' מוד' רש"י דלא מהני שליחות כמש"ל גם מה שהקשה בתומים מהא דיימר בר חשו בכתובות לא קשה מידי דשם ביתומים איירי דמטלטלי דיתמי לא משתעביד לבע"ח וע"י תפיס' רוצה להכניסו תחת שיעבוד הבע"ח ולהוציא מרשות בעל הממון ושפיר הוי יתומים בעל הממון ולא מהני שליחות בלא בעל הממון. ולפ"ז ל"ק ג"כ קושי' התו' בב"מ דף י' בד"ה ר"נ ור"ח מהא דביצה ולפי הנ"ל ל"ק דשם בביצה פי' רש"י דמיירי שעשאו שליח למלאות כיון רשם בירא דבהפקירא הוא וליכא בעל הממון מהני שליחות כמש"ל כל זה כתבתי ליישב דברי רש"י אבל העיקר כפי' התו' וסייעת' דלא מהני שליחות אפי' שכרו להיות שליח לא מהני וכדמסיק התומים ודלא כהש"ך ובש"ך שם יש ט"ס וכצ"ל וכיון דהכא החייב אינו תובע לו לא שייך לומר לאו ב"ד דידי את וגם למטה בס"ק זה צ"ל שאני פועל דידו כיד בעה"ב:
netivot_hamishpat_beurim.en: Even if he appointed him as an agent. See Shach, seif katan 1, who writes at length to reconcile Rashi, who states that when the creditor appointed him as an agent, seizure is effective even where it prejudices others. The Shach explains that Rashi means he hired him as an agent, and therefore it is effective even where it prejudices others because he is like a worker, whose hand is considered the employer's hand. See there. He overlooked the Mordechai in the first chapter of Chullin, who is uncertain whether a worker may seize a debt belonging to his employer, as Tumim cites. In my opinion, a worker cannot seize where this prejudices others. At first glance, if a worker's ability to acquire is not based on agency, since agency is ineffective where it prejudices others, but instead on the principle that the worker's hand is like the employer's hand, then even those who are legally incapable of agency, such as a deaf mute, mentally incompetent person, or minor, should, when working for another, acquire a found object for the employer. Yet no authority states this. The principal view is therefore like Tumim: the worker's hand is considered the employer's hand only where the worker himself could acquire the object, as Maharsha writes in Ketubot, Perek HaKotev. The reason is that because the worker can acquire for himself, the employer can acquire from the worker's hand. Therefore, where a deaf mute, mentally incompetent person, or minor cannot acquire for himself, the employer cannot acquire through him either. According to this, a non-Jewish worker might be effective. However, according to what I wrote elsewhere, that acquisition through despair in the case of a lost object is derived from the verse concerning an ox, a garment, and every lost object, as Tosafot write in Bava Kamma 66, and the object must come into the hand of one capable of acquiring it because the verse says, and you find it, which implies that it comes into his hand, it appears that since the verse says, every lost object of your brother, a non-Jew does not acquire a lost object through the owner's despair. Accordingly, even as a worker he would not acquire it. On this reasoning, in the law of one who seizes for his employer, where the worker has no independent hand with which to acquire it for himself, the principle that his hand is the employer's hand does not apply. Tumim likewise concludes this. As to the principal reconciliation of Rashi, it appears as follows. Nimukei Yosef in Bava Metzia, on the Mishnah concerning one who saw people running, writes that a protected courtyard, for which the owner need not be standing beside it, requires explanation. Its efficacy is not because it is considered a hand, since regarding a get even a courtyard requires proximity, nor is it because of agency, because in the name of the Ran he writes that one cannot acquire for another by agency unless he was appointed by the owner of the property, while with a found object there is no owner of the property to appoint him. Nor can one say of a courtyard, as with one who lifts a found object for another, that since he could acquire for himself he may acquire for his fellow. At first glance, why did Nimukei Yosef not simply use the Gemara's language that this is one who seizes for a creditor where others are prejudiced, since the Ran holds that even express agency does not work in such a case? The answer appears to be that Pnei Yehoshua explains that agency is ineffective where others are prejudiced because it is like agency for a transgression. But Bava Metzia 11 concludes that a courtyard can function through agency even for an actual transgression, such as theft. Therefore the Ran needed another reason, namely that monetary agency works only when the agent is appointed by the owner of the money. The Gemara did not give that reason regarding one who lifts a found object for another because the Ran may hold that acquisition for another is not based on agency and can work even where agency does not. Therefore the Gemara needed the rule that acquisition for another is ineffective where it prejudices others. Tosafot in Bava Metzia 72, however, write that even though one can acquire a found object for another, receiving money from a non-Jew does not cause the Jewish recipient to acquire it for another Jew. If the non-Jew had abandoned the money, one could acquire it for another, but where the non-Jew is transferring his own money to satisfy his debt to the lender through the borrower, the Jewish recipient would have to act as the non-Jew's agent, and there is no agency for a non-Jew. At first glance this implies that Tosafot disagree with the Ran, because they allow agency in ownerless property even without appointment by an owner. Upon examination, however, there is no dispute. I have explained elsewhere the distinction between ownerless property and an object after the owner's despair. Ownerless property has already left the owner's possession even before another acquires it, and the former owner himself must reacquire it. A lost object after despair, however, does not leave the owner's possession until it reaches the hand of one who acquires it. Tosafot therefore correctly write that agency works for ownerless property because there is no owner of the money, whereas for a found object, before it reaches the acquirer it remains the owner's, and agency without the owner is ineffective. According to this, Rashi is also understandable. One might ask the Ran: if monetary agency is ineffective without the owner of the money, why does seizure for a creditor work where it prejudices no one? The answer must be that the borrower is not regarded as the owner of the money in this respect because it is already subject to the creditor, there is no other source from which the creditor can be paid, and even by seizure the property does not entirely leave the borrower's possession, since the borrower may still discharge the debt with other money. Appointment by the owner is required only where the act removes property from the owner's possession. Therefore Rashi correctly writes that if the creditor appointed the seizer as his agent, the seizure is effective. Rashi holds that agency is effective even where it prejudices others, and the Ran's requirement of appointment by the owner of the money does not apply to seizure for a creditor because the borrower is not treated as the owner for this purpose, as explained regarding seizure that does not prejudice others, and the other creditor is certainly not the owner of the money. By contrast, Rashi agrees that agency does not work for a found object, since there is an owner of the property and agency without that owner is ineffective. This answers the Rosh's objection from the Mishnah of the rider, which concerns an appointed agent, and the commentators' objection from the baraita concerning a worker's found object, which also involves agency, because in a found object Rashi agrees that agency is ineffective as explained. Tumim's objection from Yemar bar Chashu in Ketubot is also answered, because there the case concerns heirs, and the movable property of heirs was not subject to their father's creditor. Through seizure one seeks to bring it under the creditor's lien and remove it from the possession of its owners, so the heirs are owners of the property and agency without them is ineffective. Likewise Tosafot's objection in Bava Metzia 10 from Beitzah is answered. There Rashi explains that the person appointed another as an agent to fill the vessel, and because the well is ownerless property and has no owner, agency works as explained. All this is written only to reconcile Rashi. The principal ruling, however, follows Tosafot and those who agree with them, that agency is ineffective even if he hired him as an agent, as Tumim concludes, contrary to the Shach. In the Shach there is also a scribal error. The text should read: Since here the debtor is not making a claim against him, the objection, You are not my beit din, does not apply. Later in this seif katan it should read: A worker is different, because his hand is like the employer's hand.

netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.he: חייב גם לתופס ואם תפס יותר מחובו בשביל הב"ח האחר ל"מ תפיסתו והש"ך השיג דמגו דיש לי יד לתפוס בשביל חובו זכה גם להאחר והעיקר כהסמ"ע וע"ב:
netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.en: He is also liable to the person who seized. If he seized more than the amount of his own debt for the sake of another creditor, his seizure is ineffective. The Shach disagrees and holds that through the migo that he has legal power to seize for his own debt, he also acquires on behalf of the other creditor. The primary law follows the Sema. See Beurim.

pitchei_teshuva.he: וקדם אדם אחד. עיין בת' רבינו עקיבא איגר סימן קל"ג בענין ב' בע"ח וחצר של אחד מהם היה מושכר ללוה ומת הלוה ונשארו מטלטלין בחצר ונסתפק שם אם נידון לזה המשכיר לקדם וגבה דאף לדעת הרמב"ם שהובא בש"ע לקמן סימן שי"ג ס"ג דהוי חצירו של משכיר לזכות במציאה ולדעת הש"ך שם דהרמב"ם ס"ל דבכל ענין הוי חצירו של משכיר אף שאינו דר שם מ"מ יש לפקפק בנ"ד די"ל כיון דחצר קונה מדין שליחות כדמסקינן פרק קמא דבבא מציעא דף י"ח דקטן מקטנה לא ילפינן ומבואר בהרי"ף והרא"ש שם דה"ה באיש גדול חצר דגברא לאו משום ידו הוא אלא משום שליחות אם כן יש לדון דלא מהני זכיית חצר אלא בדבר שיכול לעשות ע"י שליח אבל לענין תפיסה לגבי בע"ח אחרים לשווייה קדם וגבה דאינו יכול לעשות כן על ידי שליח. אינו יכול לעשות כן ע"י חצירו ומסיים דצ"ע לדינא ע' שם עוד והובא קצת בפ"ת לאה"ע סימן ק"ב סק"ד. וע' בספר שער משפט לעיל סימן ק"ד ס"ד שחקר ג"כ בזה ופשיט ליה דחצר עדיף משליח ומהני אף במקום שחב לאחרים מהא דחצירו קונה לו מציא' כו' ע"ש אולם בת' רע"ק שם דוחה ראיה זו חדא דזה אינו ראיה רק לשיטת תוספת שכתבו הטעם דמגביה מציאה לחבירו קנה חבירו ולא הוי תובע במקום שחב לאחרים משום דאי בעי זכי לנפשיה אם כן מוכח דחצר עדיפא משא"כ לשיטת הרמב"ן דמתרץ דמציאה לא מיקרי חב לאחרים כו' ועוד דאף לשיטת תוספת נמי אין ראיה כו' עש"ה:
pitchei_teshuva.en: And another person preceded him. Responsa Rabbi Akiva Eiger, siman 133, considers two creditors where a courtyard owned by one creditor had been rented to the debtor. The debtor died leaving movable property in that courtyard. Rabbi Akiva Eiger questions whether the landlord is deemed to have acquired the property first through his courtyard. Even according to the Rambam, cited below in siman 313, seif 3, that a landlord's courtyard can acquire found property for him, and according to the Shach there that this is so even when the landlord does not reside there, there remains a difficulty. A man's courtyard acquires by the law of agency, as Bava Metzia explains, and an act that cannot be accomplished through an agent generally cannot be accomplished through a courtyard. Since a creditor could not appoint an agent to seize property for him in a way that prejudices other creditors and thereby obtain the status of one who collected first, perhaps his courtyard cannot accomplish that result either. Rabbi Akiva Eiger leaves the practical law unresolved. Shaar Mishpat, above siman 104, seif 4, also analyzes this issue and concludes that a courtyard is stronger than an agent and may acquire even where an agent could not because the acquisition prejudices others, deriving this from the law that one's courtyard acquires found property. Rabbi Akiva Eiger rejects that proof. It works only according to Tosafot, who explain that one who lifts a found object for another acquires it for him because he could have acquired it for himself, from which one might infer that a courtyard is superior. According to Ramban, however, found property is not considered a prejudice to others at all, and even according to Tosafot the proof is not conclusive. See also the discussion cited in Pitchei Teshuva, Even HaEzer siman 102, seif katan 4.

rabbi_akiva_eiger.he: [שו"ע] ואפי' עשאו שליח וכתב. נ"ב וממילא ה"ה באם התופס זה נותנו לחצר של בעה"ח לא זכה בה כיון דחצר מטעם שליחות איתרבא הוי רק כשליח שמסר לשליח זולת בעומד בצד שדהו דהוי יד כמבואר בפ"ק דמציע' אבל לדעת הנ"י שם דחצר המשתמר בדבר שזכות היא לו הוי כיד אריכת' ועיין ש"ך לקמן סי' רמ"ג סק"י א"כ אם נתן זה התופס ליד חצר המשתמר זכה בה אבל אם נתן לחצר שאינו משתמר ואינו עומד בצד שדיהו אף לשיטת הי"א לקמן סי' ר' מ"מ הוא רק מטעם שליחות ולא מהני הכא ודוק. והגאון בעל בית מאיר השיב לי די"ל דיסוד תלב"ח דל"ק דהוי כעין אין שליח לד"ע כיון דחב לאחרים וזה ל"ש בחצר:
rabbi_akiva_eiger.en: [Shulchan Aruch] Even if he appointed him as an agent and wrote. Note: It follows that if the person who seized the property places it in the creditor’s courtyard, the creditor does not thereby acquire it. Since a courtyard acquires by virtue of agency, this is merely comparable to an agent who transferred the property to another agent, except where the creditor stands beside his field, in which case the courtyard functions as his hand, as explained in the first chapter of Bava Metzia. According to Nimukei Yosef there, however, a guarded courtyard, with respect to something that is beneficial to its owner, functions as an extended hand. See Shach below, siman 243, seif katan 10. Accordingly, if the person who seized the property places it in the creditor’s guarded courtyard, the creditor acquires it. But if he places it in an unguarded courtyard and the creditor is not standing beside his field, then even according to the opinion cited below in siman 200, acquisition is only by virtue of agency and is ineffective here. Examine this carefully. The Gaon, author of Beit Meir, replied to me that one may say the underlying rule that one who seizes for a creditor where others are harmed does not acquire is analogous to the rule that there is no agency for a transgression, because he harms others. That rationale does not apply to a courtyard.

siftei_kohen.he: מגו דאי בעי זכי לנפשיה. עמ"ש בסמ"ע ס"ק ג' וזהו דלא כמ"ש ב"י כו' וגם הב"ח חולק על הב"י וכן בתשו' משאת בנימין האריך להשיג בזה על הב"י והע"ש וזה שנים רבות חשבתי כדבריהם ועכשיו דקדקתי היטב בסוגיא פ"ק דמציעא ונלע"ד שהדין עם הב"י והע"ש דכיון דאית ליה זכייה בהגבה' זו זכי נמי לחבריה אפי' יותר ממה שיכול לזכות לעצמו דאע"ג דלא שייך מיגו דהא אפי' מ"ד דלא אמרי' מגו דבעי זכי לנפשיה זכי נמי לחבריה מודה דהיכא דזכי לנפשיה מידי זכי לחברי' אפי' מה דלא מצי למזכי לנפשיה וכדמוכח (דף ח' ע"א) מרבא דפליגא רמי בר חמא וכן (סוף ד' ט') מרב נחמן דאותיב לעולא וכפירש"י שם ע"ש דלא ס"ל מיגו ואפי' הכי סבירא ליה גבי טלית שהגביהו ביחד דאע"ג דהתם לא יוכל לזכות בטלית רק החצי שלו זכי לחבריה אידך פלגא מטעמא דכיון דזכי לנפשיה זכי נמי לחבריה ואף ע"פ שאפשר לדחוק ולחלק מ"מ אין נראה לי לחלק אלא פשטא דש"ס ריהטא כהב"י ומה שהקשה המשאת בנימין מתופס מוסירה לק"מ דהתם אינו זוכה רק מה שתופס בידו משום שתפוס בו אבל לא זכה מצד הגבהה דנימא דכיון דזכה בהגבהה זו לנפשיה זכי נמי לחבריה ודו"ק. גם מה שהוכיח המ"ב שם מהמרדכי לאו הוכחה היא דאדרב' רבותא קאמר המרדכי דאפי' אינו רוצה לתפוס לעצמו כלום יכול לתפוס לצורך חבירו. עיין בתשובת מהרשד"ם סי' שפ"א:
siftei_kohen.en: Through a migo that, had he wished, he could have acquired for himself. The Sema, Bach, and Masat Binyamin disagree with the Beit Yosef. I formerly agreed with them, but careful study of the opening chapter of Bava Metzia indicates that the Beit Yosef is correct. Once the person has a genuine right of acquisition through this act of lifting, he may acquire for another even more than he could acquire for himself. This does not depend upon an ordinary migo. Even authorities who reject the formula that one who could acquire for himself may acquire for another agree that when he actually acquires some portion for himself, the same act may acquire the remaining portion for his companion. This follows from the cases of two people jointly lifting a garment. Each can personally acquire only one half, yet each act of lifting also acquires the other half for the companion. Masat Binyamin's proof from seizure of an animal's lead is not persuasive, because there the person acquires only through physical possession of what he holds, not through an act of lifting that can operate for another. The Mordechai likewise proves the opposite of what was claimed, for it teaches that one may sometimes seize for another even without seeking any share for himself.

urim_vetumim_tumim.he: אם הלוה חייב וכו' דעת הסמ"ע דלא מצי לתפוס יותר כמו חובו אם חייב לו ק' א"י לתפוס רק ק' בשביל חבירו ולא יותר והש"ך בס"ק ב' הסכים להב"י דהואיל דיש לו יד לזכות בדבר ההוא יש לו יד לזכות יותר והביא ראיה מהך דשנים שהגביהו הטלית דאמרינן מגו דזכה לנפשיה זכה לחברי' ומשם ליכא ראיה כלל דהא יש לו יד לזכות בכל הטלית אלו הגביה אותו לבד וכיון דיש לו יד לזכות בכל הטלית זכה לחברי' אבל בחוב שלא מצי לתפוס רק במאה איך יהיה יוכל לתפוס בשביל חבירו מאתים ואולי לזה כוון הש"ך שכתב דיש לדחות בדוחק ובאמת הוא מרווח ואין כאן דוחק כלל. אבל יש ראיה לדברי הסמ"ע חדא מהך דלעיל בבור של עולי בבל דפיר"ת דאף דקי"ל המגביה מציאה קנה חבירו מ"מ הטעם משום מגו דזכיה לנפשיה ואין לו יותר מתחומו הרי דאם לזה אלף אמה מעירו ולחבירו אלפים אמה אין חבירו יוכל להוליך המים יותר מאלף אמה ולא אמרינן הואיל ויש לו יד במים יוכל לזכות לחבירו יותר ממנו כמ"ש הש"ך לענין מעות אלא ש"מ דל"א כן. ודברי ר"ת נקבעים להלכה כמ"ש בא"ח סי' שצ"ב ע"ש ברמ"א וא"כ הדין מבורר וכן מבואר מהך דב"ק דף ע' הנ"ל דקאמרינן שליח שויה ולכך אי תפיס משל נאמן מפקינן דהוי תופס לב"ח ולחד לישנא אמרינן שותפי נינהו וקאמרינן למה נ"מ למתפס פלגא הואיל והוא שותף בו וקשה א"כ כוליה לתפוס דתו לא הוי תופס לב"ח דכיון דיש לו יד במקצת ידו זוכה בכולו כמ"ש הש"ך. ועכצ"ל דזה אינו דאינו יכול לתפוס יותר מאשר תשיג ידו לתפוס בשלו וזה ברור ונכון:
urim_vetumim_tumim.en: If the debtor owes him, etc. The Sema holds that a creditor cannot seize for another creditor more than the amount of his own claim. Thus, if the debtor owes him one hundred, he may seize only one hundred on behalf of his fellow creditor, but not more. The Shach in seif katan 2 agrees with the Beit Yosef that once the person has a legal hand to acquire some of the property for himself, he may use that same hand to acquire a greater amount for his fellow creditor. He brings proof from two people who lift a garment together, where the Gemara says that because each can acquire for himself he can also acquire for the other. There is no proof from there. Each lifter had the legal ability to acquire the entire garment had he lifted it alone. Since his hand could extend to the whole garment, his acquisition can operate for the other as well. With a debt, by contrast, where one may seize only one hundred for himself, how could that limited right enable him to seize two hundred for another creditor? Perhaps this is what the Shach means when he says that the proof can be rejected with some difficulty, but in truth the distinction is broad and involves no difficulty at all. There is affirmative proof for the Sema from the case of the cisterns of the Babylonian exiles. Rabbenu Tam explains that although we hold that one who lifts ownerless property for another acquires it for him, the basis is that since the lifter could acquire it for himself, he may acquire it for the other. Consequently, the recipient cannot have a wider Shabbat boundary than the person who drew the water. If the drawer has only one thousand cubits remaining from his city while his fellow has two thousand, the fellow cannot carry the water beyond the drawer's thousand. We do not say that because the drawer has some proprietary hand in the water he can acquire for the other a greater right than he himself possesses. Rabbenu Tam's view is accepted in practice, as appears in Orach Chaim siman 392 in the Rama. The law is therefore clear. The same is evident from Bava Kamma 70. According to one version, the Gemara says the parties are partners and asks what practical consequence follows, answering that the representative may seize his half because he owns that part. If the Shach's principle were correct, he should be able to seize the whole. Once he has a right in part, his hand would supposedly extend to the remainder for the other party. The Gemara's limitation to his own half proves the opposite. A person cannot seize more for another than he himself could acquire. This is clear and correct.

urim_vetumim_urim.he:
אם הלוה חייב דעת הסמ"ע דאם חייב לתופס מאה והוא תופס בשביל אחר מאתים לאותו מנה השנית לא מהני תפיסתו דהא לא מצי לתפוס יותר מכדי חובו ומכ"ש אם באמת תפס לחובו ומבקש לתפוס הנשאר בשביל חבירו והש"ך השיג והסכים הואיל יש לו יד במקצת יש לו יד בכולו ואני בתומים הבאתי ראיה ברורה לדברי הסמ"ע ומני' אין לזוז וכ"כ המ"ב וכה"ג.
זכה בתפיסתו נראה דוקא באומר לו זכה לי או שתופס מעצמו בלי ידיעת המלוה דזכין לאדם שלא בפניו אבל אם אמר לו המלוה לך ותפס והביא לי או טול לי א"כ מגרע גרע דגלי דעתו דאין רצונו שיזכה לו ולכך לא זכה וכה"ג אמרי' גבי מציאה ועיי' לקמן סימן רס"ט ס"ו וכך הוא בגמ' וה"ה הכ' ופשוט ועיין תומים סק"א:
urim_vetumim_urim.en:
If the debtor owes him. Sema holds that if the debtor owes the person who seized one hundred, and that person seeks to seize two hundred for another creditor, his seizure helps only up to his own one hundred. He cannot seize beyond the amount of his own debt. All the more so if he already seized property for his own debt and now seeks to retain the excess for another creditor. The Shach disagrees and says that once he has a legal hand in part of the property, he has a hand in all of it. In Tumim I brought clear proof for Sema. One should not depart from his ruling. Masat Binyamin and Knesset HaGedolah likewise agree.
He was given to him, and he was given to me, or caught by himself, without the knowledge of the word, but if he said to him, “And he brought to me, and he brought me, and he brought me, or to me, from the rods of his mind, and so on, he won’t win him, and he just won.”

mechaber.he: אם הלוה אמר לאדם אחד זכה בחפץ זה לפלוני או תן מנה זה לפלוני זכה לו ואפי' אין הזוכה מכיר לאותו פלוני ואין אחד מבעלי חובות יכולים לגבות מאלו שכבר זכה בהם אחר:
mechaber.en: If the borrower told one man he had won this object to a flaw or given this dose to a panony he won and Afi does not know the same flaws and no one of the debtholders can back from those who have already received another:

baer_hetev.he: תן. לקמן סימן קכ"ה כת' הט"ו דיש פלוגתא בלשון תן אי הוה כזכי והמחבר כתב כאן תן וזכי לכל מר כדאית ליה עכ"ל סמ"ע ר"ל במתנ' וכאן מיירי גם כן מדבר מתנה. ש"ך:
baer_hetev.en: Give. Below, siman 125, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch record a dispute whether the expression 'give' has the legal force of 'acquire for him.' Here the Mechaber writes both 'give' and 'acquire,' each according to the view that applies. Sema. The Shach explains that the discussion there is about a gift, and the present case likewise concerns a gift.

beer_hagolah.he:
שם ושם ברמב"ם
טור וכך כתב הרמב"ם שם בפט"ז ממ"ש כל האומר תנו כאומר זכו דמי. ופרש"י ואין זה כשאר תופס לב"ח אלא בעל עשאו שליח לזכות בו גיטין דף י"א ע"ב
ב"י שכ"נ לו

beur_hagra.he:
אם הלוה. גטין י"א ב':
או תן. שם ולפי' ר"ת שם ד"ה כל ועוד פיר"ת כו' מיירי כאן לפלוני בע"ח וע"ל סי' ככ"ה:
ואפי' אין הזוכה. ביצה ט"ז ב' מכריז ר' יעקב כו' עד תחום שבת:
ואין אחד. כ"מ בכתובות פ"ד פ"ה א"ל את כו' תפסוה כו':
beur_hagra.en:
If the borrower... Gittin 11b.
Or "give." There, according to Rabbeinu Tam's explanation, the case is where the recipient is a creditor. See below, siman 125.
Even if the beneficiary is not... Beitzah 16b, where Rabbi Yaakov makes an announcement extending to the Shabbos boundary.
And no one... This appears from Kesubos 84-85, where a party was told to seize property.

chelkat_mechokek.he: המכר מכר ואסור להשהות'. ואם מת או גירשה קודם שכת' לה כתוב' אחרת אין לה עליו כלום:
chelkat_mechokek.en: He sold and was not allowed to stay. And if he died or sages before, he has nothing to do with him:

ketzot_hachoshen.he: אם הלו' אמר לאדם א' זכה כו' והוא מדברי הרמב"ם בפ"ק ממלו' וז"ל הרב המגיד שם כבר נתבאר בפ' י"ז שאם הי' ראובן חייב לשמעון מנה ואמר ללוי הילך לשמעון מנה זה שאני חייב לו שאם בא ראובן לחזור אינו חוזר אלמ' זכה לו וכיון שהוא אינו יכול לחזור בו ודאי אין שאר בע"ח יכולין לגבות ממנו וכן מבואר בפ"ק דגיטין דף י"א גבי הא דתופס לבע"ח דכל היכא דלו' אמר תנו נותנין עכ"ל והנה בראי' ראשונ' לא נודע כלל דהתם לא חב לאחריני וכבר הרגיש בו הלחם משנה וכת' דראי' אחרונ' היא הנכונ' דהתם הוי תופס לבע"ח במקום שחב לאחרים והיכא דאמר תנו מהני ועיקר ראייתו מן השנייה וראשונ' עשה סניף לה עכ"ל. ובעניותי גם ראי' אחרונ' איני מכיר וז"ל הש"ס בפ"ק דגיטין דף י"א ש"מ מדרבנן התופס לבע"ח קנה ואפי' במקום דחב לאחרים ופירש"י דתופס השטר וחב לבעלים אמר ר' יוחנן התופס לבע"ח במקום שחב לאחרים לא קנה וא"ת משנתינו כל האומר תנו כאומר זכי דמי והתם ודאי כיון שאינו חב אלא לבעלים והבעלים בעצמם אומרים זכה ורצו בדבר ודאי אין זה חב וגם בתופס לבע"ח אם הבע"ח אומרים זכה בשביל זה ודאי זכה אבל היכא דהלו' אומר זכה וחב לבע"ח זה לא שמענו. וגם בב"ח ראיתי שכ' על דברי הטור שכ' ואם הלוה אומר זכה בחפץ זה וז"ל מימרא דר"י בפ"ק דגיטין עכ"ל ומן התימ' שלא ביאר הראי' ואנו בעניותינו אין לנו לפרש. וגם בעיקר טעמ' דהך מילתא צריך ביאור מה בכך שהלוה אומר זכה הא מ"מ חב לבע"ח. ונראה דהרמב"ם מסברא אומר כן דהיכ' דאינו זוכה אלא בשביל חובו אז אמרינן כיון דאיכא עוד בע"ח וחב לאחריני הוי תופס לבע"ח במקום שחב לאחרים אבל הלוה בעצמו דיכול ליתן את המטלטלין לכל מי שרוצה דמטלטלין לאו בני שיעבוד נינהו ולכן בדידי' קיימא שהוא יכול ליתן את שלו במתנה למי שרוצ' ואפי' ע"י זכי' ואין זה חב לאחרים דרשאי לעשות בשלו מה שרוצה וראי' לזה נראה מסוף פ' כל הגט המלו' מעות את הכהן ואת הלוי להיות מפריש עליהן מחלקן ופריך הש"ס אע"ג דלא אתי לידי' אמר רב במכירי כהונה ושמואל אמר במזכה להן ע"י אחר וכ"כ הרמב"ם בפ"ז מה' מעשר והתם ג"כ חב לאחריני דהא טובת הנאה אינו ממון ואם תפס כהן מכהני עלמא לא מפקינן מיני' אע"כ כיון דהתור' נתנה רשות לבעלים כזה שיתנו לכל כהן שירצ' לכן בדידהו קיימא לזכות שירצה אפי' ע"י אחר וא"כ ה"ה בלוה דהתור' נתנה לו רשות ליתן את חפציו לכל מי שרוצ' לכן מזכה נמי ע"י אחר ואפי' למי שאינו חייב לו כלל ומכ"ש לבעל חוב שלו ודו"ק ולולי דמסתפינ' הייתי אומר דגם רש"י שכ' גבי תופס לבע"ח כיון שלא עשאו הנוש' שליח לאו על המלו' קאמר אלא על הלוה הוא דאמר דמלת נושה הוא שם משותף ללוה ולמלוה וע' בטעמי המצות להרב מו' מנחם הבבלי מצוה מ' בהג"ה וז"ל נושה נקרא לוה ומלו' כמו סוחר מוכר וקונה עכ"ל. וע' בתשו' הרא"ש שהובא בטור סי' ס"ה מדין שטר שנאבד ושם ג"כ הרא"ש מכנה להלו' בשם נושה ע' שם ובזה ודאי אם הלו' עשאו שליח מהני וכמ"ש אבל אם המלו' עשאו שליח גם רש"י מודה דלא מהני ולהכי ניחא דרש"י לא כ' הך דינא דעשאו שליח במגבי' מציאה לחבירו דאם עשאו שליח דמהני וגם דברי רש"י בפרק מרוב' מודה בפי' דלא מהני אם המלו' עשאו שליח גבי לא כתבינן אורכת' אמטלטלין דכפרי ע"ש ברש"י אלא הכא כיון רש"י דהנושה לא עשאו שליח היינו הלוה וראיתי במהרש"א פרק הכותב גבי יימר בר חשו דהוכיחו תוס' דאפי' שליח לא מהני ורצה ליישב דברי רש"י דגבי בע"ת כיון דלא שייך מגו דזכה לנפשי' לא מהני שליח אבל במגבי' מציא' כיון דשייך מגו דזכה לנפשי' מהני שליח ע"ש ודבריו תמוהין דהא רש"י כתבו גבי תופס לבע"ח כמ"ש רש"י מאחר שלא עשאו הנוש' שליח גם במגיני שלמה פ' הכותב כת' ליישב דברי רש"י וכת' שם דרש"י לא כת' כ"א גבי מציא' דשייך ביה מגו דזכי לנפשיה מש"ה מהני ביה נמי שליח אבל לתופס לבע"ח והרי לפנינו לשון רש"י גבי תופס לבע"ח וכמ"ש:
ketzot_hachoshen.en:
If the borrower told another person, "Acquire this for so and so," the recipient can acquire on that creditor's behalf even where other creditors are thereby disadvantaged. Maggid Mishneh cites two proofs for Rambam's rule. His first proof is from the law that if Reuven owes Shimon one hundred and gives Levi one hundred saying, "Take this to Shimon for the debt," Reuven cannot retract. That proof is not sufficient, because there no other creditor is being harmed. Lechem Mishneh therefore says the real proof is from Gittin, where the Gemara distinguishes ordinary seizure for a creditor from a case in which the owner says, "Give," and treats the latter as effective.

In my view even that proof is not clear. The Gemara's case concerns an owner instructing that property be given to the person whose right is thereby established. If the creditor himself says, "Acquire for me," that is one thing. But where the borrower says, "Acquire for this creditor," while the act harms other creditors, the Gemara does not expressly teach that the borrower's instruction overcomes the rule against seizing for one creditor at the expense of others.

The correct basis of Rambam's ruling is conceptual. Where a stranger acts only because he wishes to help one creditor collect, we say he cannot seize where the act harms other creditors. But the borrower himself may dispose of his movables as he wishes, because movables are not independently encumbered to the creditors in the same way as land. He can give his own property as a gift to anyone he chooses. Therefore he can also transfer it to a particular creditor through another person's acquisition on that creditor's behalf. The act is not treated as an improper seizure for one creditor, because the borrower is exercising dominion over his own movables.

There is a close proof from the law of tithes. A person who has lent money to a kohen or Levi can arrange that terumah or maaser be separated for that recipient, and Shmuel explains that the owner can transfer the gift to him through another person. Even though selecting one kohen necessarily disadvantages others, the Torah gave the owner the right to choose the recipient. Because the choice belongs to the owner, he can make that choice through another person's act of acquisition. The same applies to a borrower regarding his movables.

Were it not for concern about departing from the established reading, I would even suggest that Rashi's words, "since the creditor did not appoint him as agent," refer to the borrower rather than to the lender. The term used there can denote either the debtor or creditor. On this reading, Rashi means that if the borrower appoints the person to transfer the property, the transfer works, while appointment by the creditor alone does not help. This would also explain why Rashi does not use the agency rule in the case of lifting a found object for another, and it accords with Rashi elsewhere, where an authorization from the creditor does not make seizure of disputed movables effective. The later commentators who tried to reconcile Rashi by distinguishing cases where the agent could have acquired for himself do not fit the plain wording as well as this reading.
